NEW YORK (CNN) -- Former New York City police Commissioner Bernard Kerik pleaded not guilty in federal court Monday to a revised indictment charging him in a corruption and tax evasion case, according to a spokesman for the New York District Attorney. A revised indictment brings to 15 the number of counts against former police Commissioner Bernard Kerik. The revised indictment includes two new counts of aiding the filing of false returns and a charge involving making false statements while applying for a housing loan, spokesman Herbert Hadad of the district attorney's office told CNN. Kerik is accused of failing to report more than $500,000 in income between 1999 and 2004, said Patricia Haynes, the IRS agent in charge of the case. Prosecutors allege Kerik received and concealed benefits of about $255,000 in renovations to his Riverdale, New York, apartment from a company seeking to do business with the city of New York. Revisions to the original indictment, which included charges of corruption, conspiracy and tax evasion, bring to 15 the number of counts against Kerik. Barry Berke, Kerik's attorney, declined to comment. The indictment also charges that Kerik made several false statements to the White House and other federal officials when he applied for the position as adviser to the Homeland Security Advisory Council, to the Coalition Provisional Authority in Iraq and in connection with his nomination to be secretary of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. U.S. District Judge Stephen Robinson did not rule Monday on whether the two counts that include charges of lying to White House officials will be tried in Washington or White Plains, New York. Kerik is due back in court February 3 for a hearing on pretrial motions, Hadad said. A trial date has not been set. Kerik, 53, is a longtime friend and former protege of former Mayor Rudy Giuliani. President Bush nominated him to be secretary of homeland security after winning re-election in 2004, but Kerik withdrew his name amid allegations that he employed a nanny who had a questionable immigration status. Bronx District Attorney Robert Johnson began investigating allegations that Kerik had traded payment on repairs to his Bronx apartment for favors, including city contracts. The former chief pleaded guilty in 2006 to accepting tens of thousands of dollars in gifts while he worked as city corrections commissioner. He was fined $221,000 and avoided jail time under his plea agreement. Before tapping Kerik for a Cabinet post, Bush dispatched him to Baghdad to train Iraqi police after the U.S. invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein. He left three months into an expected six-month stint, with Iraqi officials telling reporters that he had completed his assignment. In 2004, he campaigned for Bush's re-election and spoke at the Republican National Convention in New York. CNN's Mary Snow contributed to this report.

# Former NYPD Commissioner Faces Expanded Federal Corruption Charges

**NEW YORK (CNN)** — Bernard Kerik, the former Commissioner of the New York City Police Department, entered a plea of not guilty in federal court on Monday to a revised indictment encompassing charges of corruption and tax evasion, according to a spokesman for the New York District Attorney's office.

The amended indictment brings the total number of counts against Kerik to 15. The revisions introduce two additional charges of aiding in the filing of false tax returns, as well as a new charge alleging Kerik made false statements while applying for a housing loan, spokesman Herbert Hadad confirmed to CNN.

According to Patricia Haynes, the IRS agent overseeing the case, Kerik is accused of failing to report more than $500,000 in income between 1999 and 2004. Prosecutors further allege that Kerik accepted and subsequently concealed benefits valued at approximately $255,000—stemming from renovations to his apartment in Riverdale, New York—from a company that was seeking to secure business with the city.

These revisions build upon the original indictment, which already contained charges of corruption, conspiracy, and tax evasion. Barry Berke, Kerik's attorney, declined to comment on the matter.

The indictment also alleges that Kerik made numerous false statements to White House officials and other federal representatives in connection with several appointments: his role as an adviser to the Homeland Security Advisory Council, his position with the Coalition Provisional Authority in Iraq, and his nomination to serve as Secretary of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.

U.S. District Judge Stephen Robinson did not issue a ruling on Monday regarding the venue for the two counts involving allegations that Kerik lied to White House officials—specifically, whether these charges will be tried in Washington or in White Plains, New York. Kerik is scheduled to return to court on February 3 for a hearing on pretrial motions, Hadad noted. No trial date has yet been established.

Kerik, 53, has long been a close friend and protégé of former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani. Following his re-election in 2004, President Bush nominated Kerik to serve as Secretary of Homeland Security; however, Kerik withdrew his nomination amid allegations that he had employed a nanny with questionable immigration status.

The current case traces back to an investigation launched by Bronx District Attorney Robert Johnson, who examined allegations that Kerik had exchanged favors—including city contracts—for repairs made to his Bronx apartment. In 2006, the former commissioner pleaded guilty to accepting tens of thousands of dollars in gifts during his tenure as the city's corrections commissioner. Under the terms of his plea agreement, he was fined $221,000 and avoided a prison sentence.

Prior to nominating Kerik for the Cabinet position, President Bush had sent him to Baghdad to help train Iraqi police forces in the aftermath of the U.S. invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein's regime. Kerik departed after just three months of an anticipated six-month assignment, with Iraqi officials informing reporters at the time that he had completed his duties. In 2004, Kerik actively campaigned for Bush's re-election bid and delivered a speech at the Republican National Convention held in New York.

*CNN's Mary Snow contributed to this report.*
